back: A table that groups data into [[imp:classes (intervals)]] and shows the number of values ([[kw:frequency]]) in each class.
It reveals patterns in large data sets.
cards.front: What is a [[kw:frequency distribution]]?

back: The distance between lower limits of consecutive classes.
$$\text{Class Width} = \left\lceil \frac{\text{Range}}{\text{Number of Classes}} \right\rceil$$
[[imp:Always round up.]]
cards.front: Define [[kw:class width]] and how to compute it.
What is the [[kw:range]] of a data set?
back: The difference between the maximum and minimum values.
$$\text{Range} = \text{Max} - \text{Min}$$
Used to find class width.

cards.front: Distinguish between [[kw:lower class limit]] and [[kw:upper class limit]].
back: [[kw:Lower class limit]]: the smallest value that can belong to a class.
[[kw:Upper class limit]]: the largest value that can belong to a class.
Classes must be non‑overlapping.

cards.front: What is the [[kw:midpoint]] of a class?
back: The average of the lower and upper class limits.
$$\text{Midpoint} = \frac{\text{Lower Limit} + \text{Upper Limit}}{2}$$
Used as a representative value for the class.
The proportion of the data that falls in a given class.
$$\text{Relative Frequency} = \frac{\text{Class Frequency } f}{\text{Sample Size } n}$$
Can be expressed as a fraction, decimal, or percent. Sum ≈ 1.
cards.front: Define [[kw:relative frequency]] and give its formula.
What is [[kw:cumulative frequency]]?
back: The running total of frequencies up to and including a particular class.
The cumulative frequency of the last class equals the total sample size $n$.
Used to construct an ogive.
A bar graph for quantitative data where bars touch.
Horizontal axis: [[imp:class boundaries]] or midpoints. Vertical axis: frequencies.
Shows the shape of the distribution.
cards.front: Describe a [[kw:frequency histogram]].
What are [[kw:class boundaries]] and how are they found for integer data?
back: Numbers that separate classes without gaps, so histogram bars touch.
For integer data: lower boundary = lower limit − 0.5, upper boundary = upper limit + 0.5.
A line graph that plots the frequency at each [[imp:class midpoint]], then connects the points.
Extend to the horizontal axis before the first class and after the last class.
Highlights the overall trend.
cards.front: What is a [[kw:frequency polygon]]?

back: A cumulative frequency graph (line graph).
Plots [[imp:cumulative frequency]] at each [[imp:upper class boundary]].
Always slopes upward; steepest part shows the class with the highest frequency.
cards.front: Define an [[kw:ogive]].

back: Same shape, but the [[imp:vertical scale]] differs.
Frequency histogram: shows counts.
Relative frequency histogram: shows proportions (decimals or percents).
Use relative histograms to compare data sets of different sizes.
cards.front: How do a frequency histogram and a relative frequency histogram differ?

back: The class with the [[imp:greatest frequency]].
It is where the cumulative frequency increases the most.
cards.front: What does the steepest part of an ogive indicate?
A data set has min=12, max=88, and you want 6 classes. What is the class width?
back: Class width = 13.
A graph that splits each number into a [[imp:stem]] (leading digits) and a [[imp:leaf]] (final digit).
Preserves original data values while showing the distribution.
Always include a key, e.g., 15 | 5 = 155.
cards.front: What is a [[kw:stem‑and‑leaf plot]]?
Advantage of a stem‑and‑leaf plot over a histogram?
back: It [[imp:retains the original data values]]; you can read exact numbers.
Histogram groups data into classes, losing individual values.
Gives a [[imp:finer view]] of the distribution, similar to using more classes.
Reveals smaller gaps and clusters.
cards.front: What does splitting stems into two rows (0‑4 and 5‑9) accomplish?

back: Each data value is represented by a [[imp:dot]] above its value on a horizontal axis.
Stacked dots show frequency. Retains original data; best for small data sets.
cards.front: Define a [[kw:dot plot]].

back: A circle divided into sectors representing categories of qualitative data.
Central angle = 360° × (class frequency / n).
Shows parts of a whole.
cards.front: What is a [[kw:pie chart]] and how do you compute sector angles?
Describe a [[kw:Pareto chart]].
back: A vertical bar graph for qualitative data, bars arranged [[imp:from tallest to shortest]] (left to right).
Highlights the most important categories; useful in business.

cards.front: When would you choose a Pareto chart over a pie chart?
back: Use a [[kw:Pareto chart]] to [[imp:rank categories]] and identify the most significant ones.
Use a [[kw:pie chart]] to emphasize proportions of a whole.
A graph of ordered pairs $(x, y)$ from two quantitative variables.
Shows the [[imp:relationship]] (association) between them.
A rising trend → positive association; falling trend → negative association.
cards.front: What is a [[kw:scatter plot]]?
Define a [[kw:time series]] and a [[kw:time series chart]].
back: [[kw:Time series]]: data collected at regular time intervals.
[[kw:Time series chart]]: plots time on the horizontal axis, connects points to show trends over time.
Scatter plot: two quantitative variables, not necessarily time; points are not connected.
Time series chart: always has [[imp:time]] on the horizontal axis; points are connected.
cards.front: How does a scatter plot differ from a time series chart?
What kind of graph is best for displaying cumulative frequencies?
back: An [[kw:ogive]] (cumulative frequency graph).
It shows the number or proportion of data values below any given upper class boundary.
Plot the frequency at each class midpoint.
Connect points with straight lines.
Extend to the horizontal axis at one class width before the first midpoint and after the last midpoint.
cards.front: How do you construct a frequency polygon?

back: Understand: min, max, range; decide number of classes (5–20).
Solve: compute class width (round up), set limits, tally frequencies.
Conclude: add midpoints, relative and cumulative frequencies, draw graphs.
cards.front: What are the steps to build a frequency distribution (blueprint)?
Which graph would you use to show the relationship between hours studied and exam score?
back: A [[kw:scatter plot]] — two quantitative variables.
Hours on horizontal axis, score on vertical axis.
The right whisker will be [[imp:longer than the left whisker]].
(This card links to measures of position in Ch 2.5, but the histogram and boxplot connection is useful now.)
cards.front: If a distribution is right‑skewed, what do you expect in a boxplot?
What should the sum of all relative frequencies be?
back: Approximately [[imp:1]] (or 100%).
Due to rounding, 0.99 or 1.01 is acceptable.
